Question:
The graph of the polynomial \[ \begin{aligned} &P(x) = x^5 + ax^4 + bx^3 \\ &\quad {}+ cx^2 + dx + e \end{aligned} \]

has five distinct \(x\)-intercepts, one of which is at \((0, 0).\) Which of the following coefficients cannot be zero?
Solution:
The intercept at the origin gives a factor of \(x\). The other four intercepts correspond to distinct nonzero real roots; call them \(r_1,r_2,r_3,r_4\). By the factor theorem, these five roots supply five linear factors. Since \(P\) has degree five and leading coefficient one,
\[
P(x)=x(x-r_1)(x-r_2)(x-r_3)(x-r_4).
\]
This form lets us find the coefficient of \(x\) without expanding the entire product. We must take \(x\) from the first factor and the constant term from each remaining factor, so
\[
d=(-r_1)(-r_2)(-r_3)(-r_4)
=r_1r_2r_3r_4\ne0.
\]
The product is nonzero because none of these four roots is zero.

To check that the other coefficients can vanish, consider
\[
x(x^2-1)(x^2-4)=x^5-5x^3+4x.
\]
Its five roots are \(0,\pm1,\pm2\), all distinct, and \(a=c=e=0\). Also,
\[
x(x^2-1)(x-2)\left(x-\frac12\right)
=x^5-\frac52x^4+\frac52x^2-x
\]
has five distinct roots \(0,-1,1,2,\frac12\) and has \(b=0\). Thus the only listed coefficient that cannot be zero is \(\boxed{d}\), choice \(\boxed{\text{D}}\).
